substeps.label: 1 · pour out
substeps.caption: After a run, with the dust settled: every lead clipped on first, then tip the container out onto the grounded stainless tray, never over paper or plastic (NFPA 484). The heap is mostly powder with a few unatomized pieces in it.

substeps.label: 2 · pieces out
substeps.caption: Container back. Pick the pieces out with tweezers: splats, beads and anything over a few millimetres go to the dish. They are feedstock again (TA 04:50), not waste.

substeps.label: 3 · onto the No. 60
substeps.caption: Cover off. A conductive scoop carries the powder to the top sieve, the No. 60 (250 µm): it scalps what the tweezers missed and keeps the No. 230 below it clean. An 8 in No. 230 takes about 35-40 g a pass (DIN 66165's 26 cm³), so a 100 g run is three passes.

substeps.label: 3 · cover on
substeps.caption: Cover on before anything is shaken: fine aluminium is a combustible dust and the cover is the containment.

substeps.label: 4 · sieve
substeps.caption: Rotate the stack in a flat circle and tap the frame, about 3 minutes (here in time-lapse). Cut open: grit stays on the No. 60, 63-250 µm on the No. 230, and under 63 µm, the print fraction, falls to the pan. Inset: the No. 230 at real size.

substeps.label: 5 · No. 60
substeps.caption: Cover off, then the No. 60: what it held joins the pieces in the dish.

substeps.label: 5 · No. 230
substeps.caption: The No. 230 next, through the funnel into its own jar: 63-250 µm, too coarse for the bed. Keep it; it can be re-atomized (E6 in #222).

substeps.label: 5 · pan
substeps.caption: The pan holds the print fraction, under 63 µm. It goes through the funnel into a jar already tared on the balance. Weigh every fraction: the yield says how many runs a print needs.

substeps.label: 6 · label, store, repeat
substeps.caption: Lids on, a 6-character ID on the print jar (#249), the jar into the desiccant box. Then the next 35-40 g from the tray. The print jar is what feeds the doser's 25 mm cartridge: the Sep 30 clog was unsieved powder.
